entry: Front part of the torso between the thorax (chest) and pelvis in humans and other vertebrates. The space it encloses is the abdominal cavity, bounded above by the thoracic diaphragm and below by the pelvic brim, and walled by three layers of abdominal muscle and the peritoneum. The cavity holds most digestive organs, including the [[Stomach|stomach]], the small intestine and the colon, as well as the [[Liver|liver]], [[Gallbladder|gallbladder]], [[Pancreas|pancreas]], [[Spleen|spleen]] and the [[Kidney|kidneys]]. The kidneys and ureters lie behind the peritoneum as retroperitoneal organs. In arthropods, the abdomen (metasoma) is the rear body section, following the thorax or cephalothorax, and in vertebrates it is also called the belly.

Ottoman sultan (r. 1876–1909), the last to exercise effective control over the fracturing empire. He promulgated the empire's first constitution in 1876, then suspended it and parliament in 1878 and ruled as an autocrat for three decades. An Islamist, he asserted his title of caliph to Muslims worldwide. His reign saw rebellions in the [[Balkans]], an unsuccessful war with the [[Russian Empire]] (1877–78) and the loss of several territories. He sponsored railways and a network of professional and military schools, but he also built a secret police and censorship system. His regime's atrocities against Armenians in 1894–97 earned him the nickname "Red Sultan." Early consensus saw his rule as stagnant; recent assessments highlight his promotion of education and public works. In 1908 the Committee of Union and Progress forced him to reinstate the constitution, and he was deposed in 1909, though his role in those events is disputed.

King of Jordan since 1999. He is a member of the Hashemite dynasty, which has ruled Jordan since 1921. He succeeded his father, King Hussein, who had named him heir a few weeks before his death. He liberalized the economy on taking the throne. After protests in 2011 he replaced the government and introduced reforms, including a return to [[Proportional representation|proportional representation]] for the 2016 election. Critics regard the changes as cosmetic, and power remains centralized in the king's hands. Abdullah promotes interfaith dialogue and is custodian of Muslim and Christian sites in [[Jerusalem]]. The 2021 Pandora Papers revealed his hidden wealth held through offshore entities.

Dutch seafarer and explorer in the service of the [[Dutch East India Company]]. He was the first European to reach [[New Zealand]], which he named Staten Landt, and he reached the coast of [[Tasmania]], naming it Van Diemen's Land after his patron. On his 1642 voyage he also reached the [[Tonga|Tonga]] and [[Fiji]] island groups. A violent encounter with the [[Māori people]] on the South Island left four of his men dead, and he made no significant contact or trade. A 1644 voyage charted the northern and western coasts of Australia and the south coast of [[New Guinea]] but found no navigable passage between them. His maps and journals influenced cartography, and knowledge from his voyages was used by [[James Cook]] more than a century later.

Group in which the result of the operation does not depend on the order of its elements. Named after the Norwegian mathematician [[Niels Henrik Abel]], such groups are also called commutative groups. The [[Integer|integers]] and the [[Real number|real numbers]] form abelian groups under addition. The concept underlies many algebraic structures, including [[Field (mathematics)|fields]], [[Ring (mathematics)|rings]] and [[Vector space|vector spaces]]. The theory is generally simpler than that of non-abelian groups, and finite abelian groups are fully classified. The fundamental theorem of finitely generated abelian groups states that each such group is isomorphic to a finite direct sum of copies of the integers and of cyclic groups of prime-power order.

Port city (pop., 2020: 198,590) in northeastern [[Scotland]], the country's third most populous city. It received royal burgh status from David I (1124–53). Its traditional industries of fishing, paper-making, shipbuilding and textiles were overtaken by oil after North Sea oil was discovered in 1969, and it became known as the offshore oil capital of Europe. Its buildings use local grey [[Granite|granite]] containing [[Mica|mica]], which gives it a sparkle. The University of Aberdeen, founded in 1495 as King's College, is the fifth oldest university in the English-speaking world.

Largest city and economic capital of [[Ivory Coast]] (pop., 2021: 6,300,000). It is the most populous French-speaking city in [[West Africa]] and the sixth most populous city proper in Africa. A new wharf in 1931 spurred its growth, and it became the capital of the French colony in 1933. The Vridi Canal, completed in 1951, made it an important seaport. It remained the capital after independence from [[France]] in 1960, and in 1983 Yamoussoukro was designated the official political capital. Abidjan still hosts many political institutions and all foreign embassies, and it is the centre of the country's economic activity.

Wife and closest adviser of [[John Adams]], second president of the United States. Mother of [[John Quincy Adams]], sixth president, she was the first second lady (1789–97) and the second first lady (1797–1801). Her letters to her husband, written while he served in the Continental Congress in [[Philadelphia]] and during the Revolutionary War, are among the most detailed accounts of the home front. She and Barbara Bush are the only women who were both the wife of one U.S. president and the mother of another. Siena College surveys of historians since 1982 have consistently ranked her among the three most highly regarded first ladies.

Partially recognized state on the eastern coast of the [[Black Sea]], internationally recognized as part of [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]]. It covers 8,665 sq km, has about 245,000 people, and its capital is Sukhumi. It was an autonomous republic within the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic when the [[Soviet Union]] began to disintegrate. The 1992–93 war left Georgia without control of most of the territory, with the ethnic cleansing of Georgians from Abkhazia. [[Russia]], Venezuela, Nicaragua and Syria recognize its independence; most other countries and the United Nations regard it as part of Georgia. Russian financial aid makes up about half of its budget. Following the [[Russo-Georgian War]] of 2008, Russia recognized Abkhazia, and the status dispute remains unresolved.

[[Discrimination|Discrimination]] and social prejudice against disabled people. Ableism characterizes people by their disabilities, regards them as inferior to non-disabled people and assigns or denies perceived abilities on that basis. It rests on [[Stereotype|stereotypes]], such as the presumption that all disabled people want to be cured, and these stereotypes justify discriminatory practices. The early 20th-century [[Eugenics|eugenics]] movement, which advocated compulsory sterilization of people with disabilities, is considered an expression of widespread ableism. The term covers [[Physical disability|physical disability]], invisible disability and [[Mental disorder|mental disorder]]; ableism directed at mental disorders is called sanism. Critics argue that the framework attributes socioeconomic gaps to bias rather than to factors such as differences in skills or health-related absence.

Political movement to end [[Slavery|slavery]] and liberate enslaved people around the world. It gained momentum in the Western world in the late 18th and 19th centuries. In 1807 the slave trade was made illegal throughout the [[British Empire]], after campaigning led by [[William Wilberforce]], and the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 freed enslaved people in the colonies after a transition period. Haiti is the only country to have self-liberated from slavery, through its revolution of 1791–1804. In the United States, the 13th Amendment in 1865 ended slavery except as punishment for crime. Brazil became the last country in the Americas to outlaw slavery in 1888. The 1948 [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]] declared slavery illegal, and Mauritania, by a 1981 decree, was the latest country to abolish it officially.

Indigenous peoples of the Australian mainland and many of its islands, excluding the Torres Strait Islanders. Humans reached Australia an estimated 50,000 to 65,000 years ago. Over time they formed as many as 500 linguistic and territorial groups, speaking more than 250 languages at the time of European colonization. Connection to ancestral territory, known as "Country," is central to their identity. Their trade networks, law and religions are among the oldest continuous cultures in the world, transmitted through stories, songlines, dance and art. The 2021 census counted 944,171 Aboriginal people, 3.7% of the population. Over 80% speak English at home, and about 77,000 speak an Indigenous language.

American psychologist known for the hierarchy of needs, a theory of psychological health in which innate human needs are fulfilled in priority, culminating in self-actualization. Maslow taught at [[Cornell University]], Brooklyn College, Brandeis University, The New School for Social Research and [[Columbia University]]. He stressed the positive qualities of people rather than treating them as a "bag of symptoms," and his work is associated with [[Humanistic psychology|humanistic psychology]]. Critics argue that the theory relies on biographical analysis of elites rather than broad experimental data. A 2002 survey in the Review of General Psychology ranked him the tenth most cited psychologist of the 20th century.

Set of monotheistic religions that revere [[Abraham]] as a patriarch and/or prophet. They include [[Judaism]], [[Christianity]] and [[Islam]], the three largest, as well as the [[Baháʼí Faith|Baháʼí Faith]], the [[Druze|Druze]] faith, [[Rastafari]] and Samaritanism. Some other religions are included by some authors, though their status is highly controversial. The term, introduced in the 20th century, replaced "Judeo-Christian" to include Islam, and some scholars argue that it oversimplifies doctrinal and cultural differences.

Material, often a mineral, used to shape or finish a workpiece by wearing away its surface through friction. Abrasives must be harder than the material they work. Natural abrasives include [[Garnet|garnet]], emery, sand and [[Diamond|diamond]]; manufactured types include fused aluminum oxide, [[Silicon carbide|silicon carbide]] and cubic boron nitride. Uses include grinding, polishing, honing, cutting, drilling and sanding. Hardness is measured on the [[Mohs scale]], on which most effective abrasives exceed 7. Superabrasives such as synthetic diamond and cubic boron nitride are the most durable and are used in precision work. Files are not abrasives, since they cut with teeth, but diamond files are a form of coated abrasive.

Region of southern Italy with a population of nearly 1.3 million. Its four provinces are L'Aquila, the regional capital; Teramo; Pescara, the largest city and main port; and Chieti. The region is mountainous in the west, with Apennine peaks such as the Gran Sasso d'Italia and the Maiella, and has beaches on the [[Adriatic Sea|Adriatic]] to the east. Half its territory is protected by national parks and reserves, more than any other Italian region, which shelter the [[Golden eagle|golden eagle]], the Marsican brown bear and the Apennine wolf. Its regional motto, *forte e gentile* ("strong and kind"), describes its character.

[[Anise|Anise]]-flavored spirit made from *Artemisia absinthium* (wormwood), green anise and [[Fennel|sweet fennel]]. It was created in the canton of Neuchâtel, [[Switzerland]], in the late 18th century, and became especially popular in late 19th- and early 20th-century [[France]], where artists and writers drank it, among them [[Charles Baudelaire]], [[Ernest Hemingway]] and [[James Joyce]]. By 1915 it was banned in the United States and much of Europe. It was portrayed as a dangerous hallucinogen, giving rise to the term absinthism, and thujone, present in trace amounts, was blamed. Its revival began in the 1990s after European Union laws removed barriers to production.

[[Monarchy|Monarchy]] in which the sovereign holds unrestricted power, unconstrained by constitutions, legislatures or other checks. Most datasets classify Brunei, Eswatini, Oman, Qatar and Saudi Arabia as absolute monarchies; some also include Bahrain, Bhutan, Jordan, Kuwait, Monaco, Morocco, Tonga, [[Vatican City]] and the United Arab Emirates. Absolute monarchies differ from constitutional monarchies, such as the [[United Kingdom]] and the Nordic countries, where the monarch's authority is limited, and from hereditary dictatorships such as [[North Korea]]. Historically they were common in Europe from the 16th to 18th centuries, notably under [[Louis XIV]] of France and [[Frederick the Great]] of Prussia. Their rulers maintain direct control over policy, justice and resources.

Lowest theoretical temperature, at which a system's internal energy, and in ideal cases its entropy, reach their minimum values. On the [[Kelvin|Kelvin]] scale it is 0 K, equivalent to −273.15 °C or −459.67 °F. The limit can be estimated by extrapolating the [[Ideal gas law|ideal gas law]] to the temperature at which a classical gas's volume or pressure becomes zero. Absolute zero can be approached but not reached. In 2018 scientists at the University of Bremen reached 38 picokelvin. Near it, matter shows [[Superconductivity|superconductivity]] and [[Superfluidity|superfluidity]]. Particles still have [[Zero-point energy|zero-point energy]] motion, as required by the [[Uncertainty principle|Heisenberg uncertainty principle]] and, for [[Fermion|fermions]], the [[Pauli exclusion principle]].

Set of spectroscopic techniques that measure the absorption of [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]] by a sample as a function of frequency or wavelength. The sample absorbs [[Photon|photons]] from the radiating field, and the variation of absorption with frequency forms the absorption spectrum. The most common arrangement directs a beam at a sample and measures the intensity that passes through. Infrared and ultraviolet–visible spectroscopy are common in [[Analytical chemistry|analytical chemistry]], where the technique identifies a substance and often quantifies it. The source, sample arrangement and detection technique vary with the frequency range and purpose of the experiment. It is also used in atomic and molecular physics, astronomy and [[Remote sensing|remote sensing]].

American art movement that emerged after World War II and centered on New York City. The term was first applied to American art in 1946 by the critic Robert Coates, and the movement gained mainstream acceptance in the 1950s, replacing the social realism of the 1930s. Key figures of the New York School included [[Jackson Pollock]], [[Mark Rothko]], Willem de Kooning, Arshile Gorky and Lee Krasner. Its gestural works and expansive color canvases drew on the emotional intensity of [[Expressionism|German Expressionism]] and the spontaneous methods of [[Surrealism|Surrealist]] artists. It was the first specifically American movement to achieve international influence, moving the center of Western art from Paris to New York.

Theoretical model of a computing system that receives inputs and produces outputs according to predefined rules. It is called a machine because it allows step-by-step execution of programs, and abstract because it ignores many aspects of physical hardware. A typical abstract machine is defined by its inputs, outputs and the allowable operations that turn one into the other. Such models serve as thought experiments in the [[Theory of computation|theory of computation]] and in analyzing the complexity of [[Algorithm|algorithms]]. Examples include finite state machines, Mealy machines, pushdown automata and [[Turing machine|Turing machines]]. They can serve purely theoretical purposes as well as model real computer systems.

Process of generalizing rules and concepts from specific examples, first principles or other methods. The result is a concept that acts as a common noun for subordinate concepts and groups related ideas into a category. For example, abstracting a leather soccer ball to the idea of a ball keeps the general attributes of balls and excludes the particulars of one ball. In a type–token distinction, a type such as 'ball' is more abstract than its tokens. Abstraction is central to Alfred Korzybski's general semantics and to mathematics and science, where it allows theorems and models to apply broadly. Philosophers from [[Aristotle]] to [[John Locke]] debated how general ideas arise from particulars.

Philosophical theory that the universe is irrational and meaningless. It holds that the human search for meaning conflicts with a seemingly meaningless world, and that this conflict makes existence as a whole absurd. Theorists differ on whether the conflict lies between human nature and the universe or within human nature itself. Its best-known proponent is [[Albert Camus]], who held that the absurd calls for defiant acceptance and who rejected [[Suicide|suicide]] as a response. Critics argue that life is in fact meaningful, or that absurdism has problematic consequences.

Rashidun caliph (r. 632–634) and closest companion of the Islamic prophet [[Muhammad]]. Muhammad's father-in-law, he was among the earliest converts to Islam, received the honorific al-Ṣiddīq ("the Truthful") and accompanied Muhammad on the migration to Medina. He led prayers in Muhammad's absence and succeeded him as caliph. He overcame the Ridda Wars, a set of uprisings, consolidating Muslim rule over the Arabian Peninsula. He launched campaigns against the [[Byzantine Empire]] and the [[Sasanian Empire]], and his successor [[Umar]] later conquered Persia and the Levant. He is credited with compiling the [[Quran]]. He died of illness after a reign of about two years, the only Rashidun caliph to die of natural causes.
